<p class="sr-only">Tensors for Machine Learning — from real data to modern models. Ravi Kalia and Sebastian Laverde Chunza.</p>

::: {.notes}
Say this out loud: nobody is expected to know tensor theory. Every new term is
defined the first time it appears. Students are ESL (Colombia) — speak slowly,
avoid idiom, and name the Spanish cognates early: eje, descomposición,
contracción, convolución.
:::

## {background-image="images/slides-final/slide-02.png" background-size="contain" background-repeat="no-repeat" background-position="center" background-color="#ffffff"}

<p class="sr-only">The workshop idea: four cards show scalar, vector, matrix and tensor as 0D, 1D, 2D and ND arrays, each defined by its shape. The guiding question of the day: before operating, what does each axis represent?</p>

## {background-image="images/slides-final/slide-02a.png" background-size="contain" background-repeat="no-repeat" background-position="center" background-color="#ffffff"}

<p class="sr-only">Four ideas, one object. The whole day in four cards. Card one: a tensor generalizes a matrix. A scalar has no axes, a vector one, a matrix two, and a tensor as many as the data needs. Card two: it holds the data. Images, video frames, taxi trips and prices are all one box of numbers, and every axis stands for something. Card three: its axes can be moved. Transpose permutes them. Reshape re-reads the same flat numbers, so the same shape can carry a different meaning. Card four: it factors. Numbers into primes, quadratics into roots, matrices into LU, QR and SVD, and tensors too. Where an inverse does not exist, the pseudoinverse answers. Carry this all day: before you operate on a tensor, name its axes.</p>

::: {.notes}
This is the map of the day, and the only slide that shows all four ideas at once. Spend a minute on it, not five. Each card is opened properly later: card 1 in section 01, card 2 in sections 02 and 03, card 3 in section 04, and card 4 in sections 07, 09, 10 and 11.

The fourth card is the one to sell. Students already factor numbers and solve quadratics. The claim is that factorization is the same move each time, applied to a bigger object. That is the promise section 09 collects on.

Say "axes", not "dimensions", from here on — and remember the "rank" warning is
due at the start of Part I.
:::

## {background-image="images/slides-final/slide-06.png" background-size="contain" background-repeat="no-repeat" background-position="center" background-color="#ffffff"}

<p class="sr-only">Map of factorizations: six matrix and tensor factorizations arranged on a ladder from LU through Cholesky, QR, SVD, Tucker and CP, each with one phrase describing what it buys.</p>
<p class="sr-only">Section 09 walks this map on real data: every factorization written as a constrained optimization, the cost of each one derived and then measured, and SVD as the best rank-k approximation there is. The "which one, and what does it cost me" question this ladder raises is answered two hours later, in the room.</p>

[📖 {{< var reading.why_so_many.title_en >}} ↗]({{< var reading.why_so_many.url >}}){.reading-tab target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer" title="Further reading on the ML blog"}

::: {.notes}
Prime factorization is unique up to ordering — the cleanest case on the slide.
Generic low-rank matrix factors have gauge freedom (the $M$/$M^{-\top}$ pair);
extra structure or a convention — positive pivots, orthonormal columns, a
positive diagonal — is what restores uniqueness for LU, QR or Cholesky. CP can
be essentially unique under suitable identifiability conditions, up to
permutation and a compensating nonzero scaling across modes; over the reals,
sign flips are a special case of that scaling. Kruskal's
$k_A + k_B + k_C \ge 2R + 2$ is a *sufficient* condition, not a necessary one,
and it says nothing about whether the decomposition is easy to find. Worth
saying if there is time: computing tensor rank is NP-hard in general, tensor
rank can exceed every individual mode dimension, and a best rank-$R$
approximation need not even exist — none of that is true of matrices.

Point forward to section 09 here. This is the minute a student wonders why
there are so many of these, and 09 is where the map gets walked with a cost
column attached.
:::

## NumPy: one buffer, different views {#numpy-memory .computing-slide .numpy-slide}

<p class="computing-lead">An <code>ndarray</code> pairs values in memory with metadata that tells us how to read them.</p>

:::: {.computing-layout}
::: {.memory-example}
```{.python code-line-numbers="false"}
import numpy as np
T = np.arange(24, dtype=np.float32).reshape(2, 3, 4)
T_t = T.transpose(2, 0, 1)
np.shares_memory(T, T_t)  # True
```

<table class="memory-table">
<thead><tr><th scope="col">Array</th><th scope="col">Shape</th><th scope="col">Strides · bytes</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><th scope="row"><code>T</code></th><td>(2, 3, 4)</td><td>(48, 16, 4)</td></tr>
<tr><th scope="row"><code>T_t</code></th><td>(4, 2, 3)</td><td>(4, 48, 16)</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>

<p class="memory-result"><strong>Same data. Reordered axes.</strong><br>Writing through the view also changes the original.</p>
:::
::: {.memory-explainer}
<p class="memory-size"><strong>96</strong> bytes</p>
<p class="memory-caption">24 values × 4 bytes per <code>float32</code><br>Both arrays share this data buffer.</p>

<dl class="concept-list">
<dt>Strides</dt><dd>Byte steps along each axis. Transpose reorders these steps.</dd>
<dt>Vectorization</dt><dd>Compiled numeric loops reduce Python overhead.</dd>
<dt>Broadcasting</dt><dd>Align shapes from the right: sizes match or one is 1. No tiled inputs.</dd>
</dl>
:::
::::

<div class="numpy-history">
<p><strong>Travis Oliphant · 2005</strong><br>Combined Numeric and Numarray to create NumPy.</p>
<p>Numeric <b>1995</b> &nbsp;→&nbsp; Numarray <b>2001</b><br>NumPy <b>2005</b> &nbsp;→&nbsp; NumPy 1.0 <b>2006</b></p>
<p><a href="https://github.com/numpy/numpy">Explore NumPy ↗</a><br>Scientific Python’s array foundation</p>
</div>

::: {.notes}
Travis Oliphant wrote Guide to NumPy and later co-founded Continuum Analytics, now Anaconda. Basic slicing and transposition return views; advanced indexing makes copies. The 96 bytes count the data buffer only, excluding array metadata.

Bridge from tensor concepts to the arrays students will manipulate in section 02.
Read the strides as byte steps: moving one position on the first axis of T skips
48 bytes. Ask which original axis becomes the first axis of T_t (axis 2).
Broadcasting avoids tiled inputs, but an operation can still allocate a large
output. Reshape may need a copy when the current strides cannot express the
requested layout. NumPy vectorization does not automatically move work to a GPU.

Sources: [NumPy internals](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/dev/internals.html),
[copies and views](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/user/basics.copies.html),
[broadcasting](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/user/basics.broadcasting.html),
[NumPy history](https://numpy.org/history/),
[Guide to NumPy](https://web.mit.edu/dvp/Public/numpybook.pdf),
[Anaconda origins](https://www.anaconda.com/about-us).
:::

## Hardware for tensor operations {#hardware-acceleration .computing-slide .hardware-slide}

<div class="hardware-intro">
<p class="computing-lead">The workload determines which architecture helps.</p>
<p class="hardware-equation"><span>D = AB + C</span><br>Matrix multiply–accumulate</p>
</div>

<table class="hardware-table">
<colgroup><col style="width:20%"><col style="width:30%"><col style="width:28%"><col style="width:22%"></colgroup>
<thead><tr><th scope="col">Architecture</th><th scope="col">How it computes</th><th scope="col">Best suited to</th><th scope="col">Memory examples</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><th scope="row"><strong>CPU</strong><span>General purpose</span></th><td>Multiple cores + SIMD<br><small>Flexible control flow</small></td><td>General tasks<br>Low latency</td><td>Caches + DDR DRAM</td></tr>
<tr><th scope="row"><strong>GPU</strong><span>NVIDIA</span></th><td>SIMT + Tensor Cores<br><small>CUDA programming platform</small></td><td>Parallel contractions<br>Matrix multiply–accumulate</td><td>GDDR or HBM</td></tr>
<tr><th scope="row"><strong>TPU</strong><span>Google · custom ASIC</span></th><td>Systolic matrix units (MXUs)<br><small>Operands pass between neighbors</small></td><td>Dense matrix products<br>Reuse data across operations</td><td>On-chip buffers + HBM</td></tr>
<tr class="other-hardware"><th scope="row">Other ML ASICs</th><td>Specialized dataflow</td><td>Target workloads</td><td>SRAM, DRAM or HBM</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>

<p class="hardware-caveat">Memory and supported precision vary by device generation.</p>

<div class="computing-takeaway"><strong>Moving data costs time.</strong><span>Reuse data on the device. Small operations and repeated transfers can erase the speedup.</span></div>

::: {.notes}
Memory bandwidth limits many elementwise operations; large, well-tiled matrix products may be compute-bound. Volta example: a Tensor Core performs a 4×4 matrix multiply-accumulate per clock with FP16 inputs and FP32 accumulation. Later generations differ.

SIMD means single instruction, multiple data. SIMT means single instruction,
multiple threads. A systolic array passes operands between neighboring processing
elements rather than repeatedly fetching every operand from memory. It still
needs buffers and memory transfers. HBM means high-bandwidth memory.

The 4-by-4 operation per clock describes a Volta Tensor Core's throughput,
not the latency of an arbitrary matrix product or a rule for all GPU generations.
The table gives memory families rather than implying that every CPU uses DDR5
or every GPU uses HBM3e. TPU is itself an application-specific integrated circuit.

Sources: [NVIDIA GPU performance guide](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/performance/dl-performance-gpu-background/index.html),
[Volta Tensor Cores](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/programming-tensor-cores-cuda-9/),
[Google TPU architecture](https://docs.cloud.google.com/tpu/docs/system-architecture-tpu-vm).
:::

## Numerical libraries & ML frameworks {#numerical-software-stack .computing-slide .framework-slide}

<p class="computing-lead">Familiar tensor operations sit above optimized numerical routines.</p>

:::: {.computing-layout}
::: {.library-column}
<h3>Inside a NumPy operation</h3>

<div class="operation-row"><code>A @ B</code><span>Matrix product</span><strong>BLAS</strong></div>
<div class="operation-row"><code>np.linalg.svd(A)</code><span>Singular value decomposition</span><strong>LAPACK</strong></div>

<table class="blas-table">
<caption>BLAS · standard operations at three levels</caption>
<thead><tr><th scope="col">1 · Vector</th><th scope="col">2 · Matrix–vector</th><th scope="col">3 · Matrix–matrix</th></tr></thead>
<tbody><tr><td>Dot product</td><td>y = Ax</td><td>C = AB</td></tr></tbody>
</table>

<p class="library-detail"><strong>LAPACK builds on BLAS</strong> for linear systems, SVD and eigenproblems.</p>
<p class="accelerator-libraries"><strong>Accelerator libraries</strong><br>cuBLAS · GPU BLAS<br>cuTENSOR · tensor contractions<br>oneDNN · neural network primitives</p>
:::
::: {.framework-column}
<h3>Frameworks add more</h3>

<p class="framework-capabilities">Automatic differentiation · device placement · compilation</p>

<dl class="framework-list">
<dt>PyTorch</dt><dd>Dynamic autograd<br><code>torch.compile</code></dd>
<dt>JAX</dt><dd>Composable transformations<br><code>jit</code> · <code>vmap</code> · <code>grad</code></dd>
<dt>TensorFlow</dt><dd>Eager execution + graphs<br><code>tf.function</code></dd>
<dt>Keras 3</dt><dd>Model API over<br>TensorFlow / JAX / PyTorch</dd>
<dt>Haiku / Flax</dt><dd>Neural network modules on JAX</dd>
</dl>
:::
::::

<div class="computing-takeaway"><strong>Name the axes. Check the shapes.</strong><span>Those habits transfer across frameworks.</span></div>

::: {.notes}
LAPACK succeeded LINPACK and EISPACK. Tensor decomposition libraries reuse matrix routines. JAX pure functions support tracing and XLA compilation. TensorFlow includes tools for serving models. Haiku and Flax manage neural network parameters. The NumPy examples can dispatch to optimized libraries; they do not guarantee a particular backend.

BLAS is an interface with multiple implementations, such as OpenBLAS and MKL.
LAPACK supplies matrix algorithms, not general tensor factorization algorithms.
Dispatch depends on the operation, dtype, layout and installed backend. A
framework may use vendor libraries or generate its own kernels. oneDNN is a
neural network primitive library, not a drop-in BLAS implementation.

Connect this back to the next section: before choosing a backend, name the axes
and check shapes. Those habits transfer across frameworks.

Sources: [BLAS](https://www.netlib.org/blas/),
[LAPACK introduction](https://www.netlib.org/lapack/lug/node5.html),
[cuBLAS](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cublas/),
[cuTENSOR](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cutensor/latest/),
[oneDNN](https://uxlfoundation.github.io/oneDNN/),
[PyTorch autograd](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/notes/autograd.html),
[JAX concepts](https://docs.jax.dev/en/latest/key-concepts.html),
[TensorFlow graphs](https://www.tensorflow.org/guide/intro_to_graphs),
[Keras 3](https://keras.io/keras_3/),
[Haiku](https://dm-haiku.readthedocs.io/en/stable/),
[Flax](https://flax.readthedocs.io/).
:::

Objective: distinguish wide, square and tall matrices and use the pseudoinverse for stable solutions. Three colour-coded matrices illustrate each case.</p>

## {background-image="images/slides-final/slide-20a.png" background-size="contain" background-repeat="no-repeat" background-position="center" background-color="#ffffff"}

<p class="sr-only">Three shapes, three answers, in four cards. A square full-rank matrix: the inverse exists, and Ax = b has exactly one solution. A square singular matrix: the inverse is undefined, but the pseudoinverse is not, because it is computed from the SVD. A tall matrix, more equations than unknowns: A-plus b is the least-squares fit that minimises the residual. And a wide matrix, infinitely many solutions: A-plus b returns the one of smallest norm.</p>
[Colab ↗]({{< var repo.colab_base >}}/07-inverses-and-pseudoinverse.ipynb){.colab-tab target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer" title="Open notebook 07 in Google Colab"}

and make the room say which case California Housing is before the next slide
shows it.

## {background-image="images/slides-final/slide-21a.png" background-size="contain" background-repeat="no-repeat" background-position="center" background-color="#ffffff"}

<p class="sr-only">What about tensors? Three cards. First: no tensor inverse is in common use. That is a fair question with an honest answer, not a gap in your reading. Second: definitions do exist, built on the Einstein product and on the t-product for order-3 tensors, and they are active research. Third: in practice you unfold the tensor into a matrix, apply the matrix pseudoinverse, and fold the result back. A 4 by 3 by 5 tensor unfolds to 4 by 15, whose pseudoinverse is 15 by 4. M A-plus M returns M exactly, because unfolding loses nothing.</p>
<p class="sr-only">This is also where the second half's through-line starts: the pseudoinverse in section 07, Richardson-Lucy deconvolution in section 09 and Tucker in section 10 are three instances of one idea — when a problem has no exact answer and no true inverse, find the best stable approximation instead.</p>
[Colab ↗]({{< var repo.colab_base >}}/07-inverses-and-pseudoinverse.ipynb){.colab-tab target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer" title="Open notebook 07 in Google Colab"}

[📖 {{< var reading.inverses_practice.title_en >}} ↗]({{< var reading.inverses_practice.url >}}){.reading-tab target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer" title="Further reading on the ML blog"}

::: {.notes}
"Is there a tensor inverse?" gets asked in every run of this workshop. Answer
it here instead of deflecting: there is no single one, several definitions do
exist, and the working answer is unfold, pinv, fold back.

State the through-line here as well as on the closing slide. Sections 08, 09
and 10 all sit downstream of it, and saying it now is what keeps the second
half from reading as four unrelated blocks.
:::

<p class="sr-only">Factor once, solve many: the same real least-squares problem three ways. Normal equations are fastest to write, and they square the condition number. QR is the stable default, and never forms A-transpose-A. SVD is the most expensive and the most informative, because Eckart-Young gives the truncation error without building the truncation.</p>

lesson. What survives the machine is the ratio between methods at a fixed
size — a full SVD near 39 times a Cholesky — not the exponent, which comes in
under 3 because of parallelism and cache.

## {background-image="images/slides-final/slide-29b.png" background-size="contain" background-repeat="no-repeat" background-position="center" background-color="#ffffff"}

<p class="sr-only">Four decompositions, four bargains. CP stores a sum of rank-1 components, R times I plus J plus K numbers, and is the choice when the components have to be read one by one. Tucker stores one subspace per mode plus a core, and is the choice when each mode needs a rank of its own. Tensor Train stores a chain of small cores, growing only linearly with order, and is the choice when a dense core would explode. And t-SVD takes an FFT along mode 3, matrix SVDs, and an inverse FFT, and is the choice when the third mode carries a meaning of its own.</p>
[Colab ↗]({{< var repo.colab_base >}}/11-tensor-factorizations.ipynb){.colab-tab target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer" title="Open notebook 12 in Google Colab"}

::: {.notes}
Read the four headings in order and let the room ask which one their own data
wants. That question is the section; the arithmetic is not.

The two meanings of "rank" collide here — Chapter 2's independent columns and
the tensor sense. Say which you mean every time.
:::
